Chapter 32

Notes: Tiptap through an attachment

Tiptap has no Svelte binding and needs none: {@attach tiptap()} hands it the element and destroys it on cleanup. A debounced command saves the JSON; a counter makes isActive() reactive for the toolbar; remote edits arrive through the live query and are applied only when the person is not mid-sentence.

By the end of this chapter

Integrate an imperative editor library with an attachment, make its non-reactive API drive a toolbar, and merge remote changes without stamping on someone typing.

Tiptap’s Editor takes a DOM element and owns it. That is exactly the contract of a Svelte attachment: a function that receives the element when it is in the document and returns a cleanup for when it is not. No onMount, no bind:this — and no wrapper library, because there is nothing for one to add. One rule comes with the contract, though, and the first version of this file broke it: an attachment runs inside an effect, so any state it *reads* while it runs is a reason to run it again — to call its cleanup and start over.

The attachment creates the editor with the note from the live snapshot, the editable flag from the viewer’s role, and two callbacks: onUpdate schedules a save, onTransaction bumps a counter. All of that is read inside untrack(() => new Editor(…)), which reads without depending — the comment above the function tells the story of what happened without it. What may change later gets an effect of its own. editable is a prop, so a child $effect inside the attachment follows it with setEditable, and Svelte ties that effect to the attachment and stops it with the attachment; the note a companion saves arrives through the effect after the function. The extensions are StarterKit and Placeholder, which writes the empty-note sentence from the message file onto the first empty paragraph as data-placeholder for the CSS to draw. The cleanup destroys the instance — and first sends a save that is still waiting for its pause, rather than throwing it away with the editor; save() reads the editor’s JSON before its first await, so the save sent from the cleanup reads a live editor. editor is $state.raw because a Tiptap editor is a large object with its own internal state and must not be proxied — raw stores the reference and signals only on reassignment.

Why untrack, and what the first version did

The first version read view.document.note and editable straight into new Editor({…}). That looks harmless — the values are only *used* once — but the attachment’s effect cannot tell using from depending: whatever it read, it now depends on. view.document is a new object with every snapshot of the live query, and a snapshot comes after every save, this person’s own included, and whenever a companion arrives or points at a stop. Each one destroyed the editor and built another: the cursor gone, the undo history gone, the save that was waiting for its pause cancelled by the cleanup’s clearTimeout, and the next keystrokes typed into nothing. The end-to-end test for notes typed once and waited for “Saved”, so it never typed *after* a snapshot and could not see it. Svelte’s documentation names both ways out, under “Controlling when attachments re-run”: read the starting values without tracking them, and apply later changes from a child effect. Chapter 46 has the test that types, waits for the save and for a companion to arrive, and carries on typing without clicking.

Two small mechanisms. Saving is a debounce — type, pause eight hundred milliseconds, one command with the whole document, validated by the same NoteDocSchema the server checks so a too-long note is refused before the request. And the effect handles the other direction: when the live document carries a note somebody else saved, replace the editor’s content — but only when this person is not focused in it, which is what “mid-sentence” means here. Last writer wins on a page two people rarely edit at the same moment; the comment says which project has the CRDT.

editor.isActive("bold") is not reactive; it is a method on an object Svelte knows nothing about. The counter is the bridge: every Tiptap transaction increments transactions, the $derived.by reads it — void transactions is the read — and so recomputes after every edit, and the toolbar buttons follow the cursor. The tools array is data: a key, a message function for the label, an icon, and a command chain, rendered by one {#each}. A pressed tool is drawn three ways — a tier-3 pill, the 1px --segment-edge, and the icon at bold weight — because in the dark theme the tier step alone is 1.1:1, and Bold looked the same on and off.

Why not a Svelte wrapper for Tiptap

Several exist. Each is a component that calls new Editor in onMount and exposes the instance through a store or a prop — which is what the forty lines of tiptap() do, with an attachment’s cleanup semantics for free. A wrapper would add a dependency, a version to track against Tiptap’s own, and an abstraction between you and the editor’s excellent API. The rule from chapter 01: could we remove it later? Here there was nothing to add in the first place.

Checkpoint

  • You can write an attachment for a library that owns an element and say what the cleanup must do.
  • You can say why state read inside an attachment re-runs it, and how untrack and a child $effect keep an editor alive through a live document’s snapshots.
  • You can explain the counter that makes a non-reactive API reactive.
  • You can say when a remote note replaces the editor’s content and when it does not.
